title: Bounded Adjustment with Reliability-Guided Embedding for Imbalanced Learning with Noisy Labels
abstract: Class-balanced learning and label noise create a coupled failure mode: frequency correction prevents majority classes from dominating the decision rule, but can amplify incorrectly labeled minority examples. We introduce BARGE (Bounded Adjustment with Reliability-Guided Embeddings), a single-stage objective combining a bounded, prior-adjusted density-power score with reliability-guided angular geometry. Its classification score is strictly proper in the adjusted probability space and recovers balanced Bayes ordering under clean supervision and the true class prior. Under label contamination, its finite range bounds classification-risk perturbation at a fixed predictor, while its logit gradient redescends when the model confidently contradicts the supplied label. The adjusted target probability also weights class-equal feature compactness, and a one-sided separation term discourages aligned class directions. BARGE requires neither a noise rate nor a transition matrix, uses one network, and leaves inference unchanged. We evaluate it on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet under long-tail and step imbalance, clean labels, and 20% and 40% random incorrect-label replacement. Across 12 clean settings, BARGE ranks second overall and attains the lowest error in four. Under corruption, it achieves the lowest mean balanced error in all six dataset-corruption settings, reducing the six-setting average from 72.32% for the strongest competitor to 70.00%. It also obtains the highest macro-F1 and macro-AUPRC in every corrupted-label setting. Ablations show that class-equal angular compactness improves on the bounded score alone. These results support bounded predictive influence and reliability-guided geometry as complementary mechanisms for imbalanced learning with uncertain labels.

title: TEAR: Table Extraction with Attribute Recommendation from Texts via Large Language Models
abstract: Table extraction from texts is an important task for information systems, and recent approaches that prompt large language models (LLMs) with instructions have drawn great attention for their strong performance. Existing works have assumed the input texts to be table descriptions or specialized documents. However, these efforts have largely overlooked another prevalent category of texts, commonly found in news reports and social media: naturally occurring texts. Extracting tabular information from such texts poses two distinct challenges. First, high variability and the absence of explicit structural cues make fixed heuristic LLM prompts limited in precisely delineating extraction boundaries. Second, manually predefined schemas cannot capture open-ended, unseen attributes in naturally occurring text. In this paper, we propose a framework, TEAR, to address these challenges. It comprises two synergistic workflows: a Table Extraction Workflow that dynamically adapts instructions to overcome the limitation of heuristic instructions, and an Attribute Recommendation Workflow that discovers new attributes from texts to complement the heuristic schema. To our knowledge, TEAR is the first framework that supports automated text-driven attribute recommendation, enabling exploratory schema design for table extraction. To evaluate TEAR, we establish the benchmark for table extraction and attribute recommendation on naturally occurring texts, including two real-world datasets, manual annotations, appropriate metrics, and baseline comparisons. Experiments show that TEAR achieves state-of-the-art performance on both tasks, and the recommended attributes effectively enhance extraction performance in exploratory scenarios.

title: ER-EDF: A Psychology-Grounded Emotion Regulation Framework for Speech Empathetic Dialogue Generation in Large Audio-Language Models
abstract: Empathetic response generation in spoken dialogue systems requires both accurate emotion perception and appropriate emotion regulation. Grounded in psychological theories such as the Perception-Action Model and emotion regulation theory, effective empathy depends not only on inferring a user's affective state but also on regulating how it is expressed in responses. However, recent large audio-language models (LALMs) largely treat emotion as a direct conditioning signal, lacking explicit regulatory mechanisms, which often leads to affect mirroring rather than calibrated support. We propose ER-EDF, a psychology-grounded framework that explicitly decouples emotion perception and emotion regulation in LALMs. Perception tracks the user's emotional state, while regulation determines how this state should guide empathetic response generation. The framework is model-agnostic and integrates seamlessly into existing LALMs. We further construct a spoken empathetic dialogue dataset and introduce empathy-aware evaluation metrics beyond lexical matching. Experiments across five LALMs and two datasets show that ER-EDF consistently improves empathetic response quality in both automatic and human evaluations, highlighting the importance of jointly modeling emotion perception and regulation in spoken empathetic dialogue systems, paving a new direction for psychologically grounded empathetic AI.

title: THE LOGIC OF LEARNING MACHINES - How Artificial Intelligence Sees, Learns, Reasons, and Creates
abstract: The Logic of Learning Machines: How Artificial Intelligence Sees, Learns, Reasons, and Creates is a comprehensive educational textbook and reference work introducing the foundations, methods, applications, limitations, and future directions of artificial intelligence.Written for students and readers who want to progress from introductory concepts to technically substantial material, the book begins with the fundamental questions of what artificial intelligence is, how computers represent information, and how systems learn from data. It then develops the major ideas of machine learning, including supervised and unsupervised learning, neural networks, deep learning, computer vision, speech processing, and representation learning.The book provides an extensive treatment of modern generative artificial intelligence, including language modeling, Transformers, large language models, tokenization, attention, inference-time computation, post-training, multimodal systems, image, audio and video generation, retrieval-augmented generation, tool use, memory, and AI agents.Later sections examine the engineering and evaluation of intelligent systems, including the AI development lifecycle, data quality, reproducibility, model and system evaluation, calibration, uncertainty, benchmark design, robustness, hallucinations, failure analysis, deployment, monitoring, and the distinction between model performance and real-world system performance.The social and responsible-use dimensions of AI are also covered in depth, including bias and fairness, privacy, security, misinformation and deepfakes, copyright, ownership, governance, accountability, and the use of AI in education, medicine, science, work, and creativity.The final part explores reinforcement learning, sequential decision-making, robotics, planning, reasoning, memory, autonomous systems, multi-agent systems, AI safety, alignment, interpretability, scalable oversight, AI control, frontier-model evaluation, automated AI research, recursive self-improvement, and evidence-based scenarios for the future of artificial intelligence.Throughout the book, emphasis is placed on understanding mechanisms rather than treating AI as a black box. Technical concepts are connected to practical examples, mathematical foundations, implementation considerations, case studies, exercises, review questions, applied challenges, and critical evaluation of AI claims.The volume also includes capstone projects, an extensive glossary, an appendix covering the mathematics required for AI, a Python quick-start guide, and a dedicated guide to interpreting AI benchmarks and model comparisons.The intended audience includes undergraduate students, independent learners, educators, software and computing professionals, and readers seeking a broad but technically grounded understanding of contemporary artificial intelligence.First Edition, 2026.

title: A Research Framework for Artificial Cognition Based on Temporal–Causal Loops (White Paper V1.0)
abstract: This white paper presents an exploratory research framework for artificial cognition developed upon the conceptual foundation of the XiaoWeiyang Artificial Cognitive System Theory. Transitioning from the theoretical inquiry of "what artificial cognition is" to "how artificial cognition emerges," this initiative formalizes the "Temporal–Causal Loop" paradigm. The paper investigates whether temporal continuity and causal relationships can serve as an essential foundation for the emergence of artificial cognition across sustained operational lifespans. This public document discloses the foundational premises, conceptual taxonomy, four-tier research framework, academic positioning, and current empirical milestones. It establishes a formal boundary between open research paradigms and proprietary low-level engineering implementations. The publication serves as milestone documentation and establishes academic priority for the Temporal–Causal Loop trajectory while maintaining strict adherence to empirical falsifiability: proposing research directions without presupposing dogmatic outcomes.

title: Zero-Trust Multi-Tenant Orchestration for Distributed LLM Workloads: A High-Performance DevSecOps Framework Using RDMA and Hardware Enclaves
abstract: As Large Language Model (LLM) training and inference transition to multi-tenant cloud environments, ensuring cryptographically isolated workload environments without sacrificing network throughput remains a paramount challenge. Traditional encryption-in-transit mechanisms introduce substantial CPU overhead, severely degrading inter-node communication speeds. In this paper, we propose a novel high-performance DevSecOps framework that integrates Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) over Converged Ethernet (RoCEv2) with hardware-enforced Confidential Virtual Machines (CVMs). By establishing zero-trust orchestration policies within continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines, our architecture offloads security handshakes and memory access isolation directly to hardware enclaves and SmartNICs. Experimental evaluation indicates that our proposed framework reduces gradient synchronization latency by up to 41% compared to standard TLS-over-TCP pipelines, while maintaining strict memory and network isolation boundaries across multi-tenant environments.⁠

title: The AI-Enabled Scientific Frontier
abstract: As artificial intelligence's capabilities improve, it is increasingly viewed as a general scientific method. But how true are these claims? Does AI outperform all techniques, or only some, and how is this changing? To assess the claims, we assemble a corpus of 2,507 head-to-head comparisons between AI and other scientific analysis techniques across 27 scientific disciplines from papers published between 2000 and early 2025. We find a profound dichotomy. Relative to traditional statistics, AI often outperforms, but at a significantly higher computational cost. But there are also nearly a quarter of cases where AI is both more expensive and performs worse than traditional statistical techniques and this fraction has been stable for a decade. Relative to scientific computing, AI often underperforms, but at lower computational cost. This has begun to change: since 2020, AI's performance against scientific computing has notably strengthened and it now outperforms on more than half of comparisons. These patterns suggest that AI is therefore not a universal replacement for existing methods, but rather a valuable -- and improving -- part of a new AI-enabled scientific frontier.

title: Approval Integrity and Recovery in LLM Answer Publication
abstract: Publication integrity in LLM systems requires binding approved content to its current authorization context. We examine exact-content binding, authorization freshness and checkpoint recovery in Lightcap's publication enforcement mechanism. On 900 independently human-annotated RAGTruth responses from 150 source tasks, three dated Ministral models and a same-model direct-grounding baseline yield 3,600 assessments. The production response-act checker instantiated with 14B accepts 291 of 302 unsupported-labelled answers; the direct baseline accepts 41. Supported-answer retention is 95.2% and 66.9%, respectively. An exact promotion-correction identity tracks error through 100 chronological 3B-14B-8B-14B answer trajectories. Among 65 initially approved answers, the final stateful recheck-recovery policy increases exact-match error by 9.23 percentage points relative to the initial checkpoint (95% article-clustered interval [-1.72, 19.61]). Controlled evidence-fingerprint changes expose asymmetric freshness enforcement between publication and recovery. A separate BIPIA prompt-injection experiment records zero target insertions among 266 valid editor outputs. External Hugging Face calibration experiments transfer retrieval models from ArguAna to SciFact and NFCorpus, and diagnostic decision rules from Thunderbird to BGL, distinguishing probability calibration from ranking changes. The measurements separate semantic false approval, stale authorization and recovery-induced error at executable publication boundaries.

title: What Does an LLM Learn from Reinforcement Learning? A Mechanistic Interpretability Perspective with Fixed-SAE Track
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is widely utilized in large language model training to improve targeted capabilities, yet how RL reshapes a model remains poorly understood. Prior attempts to explain how RL works largely offer behavioral perspectives, leaving open what RL gives a model at the representation level: can RL create genuinely novel features, and which existing features does it enhance or suppress? Recent developments in mechanistic interpretability suggest sparse autoencoders (SAEs) as a promising lens to decompose internal activations into human-interpretable features; however, they cannot be directly applied to tracking change across training. In this work, we introduce Fixed-SAE Track, a framework that trains one shared SAE per considered layer on activations pooled across the base model and all RL checkpoints, holding every feature direction fixed so that representation shifts are rigorously defined through the activations of interpretable SAE latents, including the detection of emerging novel features. Validated across multiple datasets and RL algorithms, we find that RL-induced drift is small, gradual, concept specific, and concentrated in late layers, mainly enhancing the sampling rates of a small set of ladder tokens, formatting scaffolding such as step breaks and answer delimiters, rather than reshaping problem content. Steering these features into the base model recovers around 80% of RL's performance gain, suggesting that RL primarily elicits capabilities the model already possesses, much as steering does. We further design a synthetic benchmark with features known by construction to test whether RL can instill genuinely novel features. We believe Fixed-SAE Track provides a principled approach to tracking representation shifts and offers representational evidence for understanding how reinforcement learning changes the inner representation of LLMs.

title: A positive-definite Fourier transform, with applications to fractional Brownian motions and Bayesian probabilistic numerics
abstract: This article is motivated by the use of Bayesian probabilistic numerics for the construction of numerical schemes for PDEs. To avoid the "flat limit problem" encountered for this problem, we consider Gaussian process priors with homogeneous covariance kernels. To construct such kernels, we introduce the positive definite Fourier transform, which defines an invertible map on the set of tempered positive semi-definite distributions onto itself. This enables us to construct an extension of the fractional Brownian motion kernel with arbitrary Hurst parameter H > 0, and arbitrary space dimension R^d , d > 0. Using such kernels, we show that Gaussian process regression with such kernels and with unknown polynomial mean function is mathematically equivalent to interpolation with fractional polyharmonic splines. This finally allows us to construct numerical schemes for the scalar linear transport equation, which exhibit fractional convergence rates fornon-smooth initial data.

title: Feature Selection-Assisted Support Vector Machine Classification of Breast Cancer Mammographic Outcomes
abstract: Aims: This study assessed the effect of feature selection on Support Vector Machine classification of breast cancer mammographic outcomes using image-derived mammographic predictors. Study Design: The study adopted a secondary-data comparative statistical learning design. Place and Duration of Study: The study used the publicly available Curated Breast Imaging Subset of the Digital Database for Screening Mammography. The analysis was conducted at the Department of Mathematics, Multimedia University of Kenya. Methodology: After image matching and preprocessing, 2,863 training observations and 704 testing observations were retained. Thirty-four image-derived predictors were extracted from cropped mammogram images and region of interest masks. The predictors comprised texture, shape and intensity features. Correlation-Based Feature Selection and Elastic Net-regularised multinomial logistic regression were applied before radial basis function Support Vector Machine classification. Model performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, macro F1-score, weighted F1-score and McNemar’s test. Results: Correlation-Based Feature Selection retained five predictors, reducing the feature space by 85.3%. Elastic Net retained sixteen predictors after coefficient ranking and cross-validated subset selection, reducing the feature space by 52.9%. Elastic Net-SVM achieved the highest accuracy of 0.5369, while the baseline SVM trained on all extracted predictors achieved the highest macro F1-score of 0.5200. McNemar’s tests showed no statistically significant differences in paired classification error rates among the three SVM models at the 5% level. Conclusion: Feature selection reduced the input feature space and improved model interpretability but did not produce a statistically significant improvement in overall SVM classification performance. The findings highlight the need to report class-level performance, particularly malignant recall, when evaluating feature selection-assisted mammographic classification models.

title: Comparing Classical Hopfield Networks and a Hybrid Quantum-Classical Associative Memory Model: Recall Accuracy, Noise Robustness, and Storage Capacity
abstract: Associative memory, the ability to reconstruct complete information from partial or noisy cues, is a defining feature of human cognition and an enduring objective in artificial intelligence. Classical neural models such as Hopfield networks have long provided insight into distributed storage and retrieval mechanisms, yet they remain constrained by limited storage capacity and susceptibility to noise. Recent developments in quantum computing have motivated investigation of hybrid quantum-classical architectures as alternative approaches to memory representation and retrieval. This study examines how effectively hybrid quantum-classical models can reproduce associative memory functions compared to Hopfield networks, with a particular focus on recall accuracy under varying noise levels, storage capacity, and computational efficiency. Through small-scale experiments using binary patterns and hybrid quantum circuits, we evaluate potential quantum advantages and practical trade-offs. The findings contribute to ongoing discourse in quantum machine learning and cognitive modeling, underscoring both the promise and current limitations of quantum-inspired associative memory systems. Our guiding research question is: To what extent can hybrid quantum–classical models replicate associative memory functions more effectively than classical neural memory models, particularly in terms of recall accuracy under noise and storage capacity?

title: The Human-AI Resonance Protocol 2.0 A Testable Framework for Representational Coherence, Intention Translation, Mutual Prediction, Adaptive Coupling, and Civilizational Co-Evolution
abstract: Description The Human–AI Resonance Protocol 2.0 (HARP 2.0) develops a comprehensive framework for studying how human beings and artificial intelligence systems can establish stable, interpretable, adaptive, and correctable forms of cognitive cooperation. The central premise is that Human–AI resonance is not identical to alignment, agreement, obedience, or synchronization. Two heterogeneous cognitive systems do not need to think alike in order to cooperate effectively. What they require is sufficiently accurate mutual representation, interpretable intention exchange, predictive coordination, feedback, repair, and the ability to preserve meaningful differences without collapsing into confusion or domination. The original HARP framework identified three fundamental barriers to Human–AI cooperation: cognitive distance, representational mismatch, and divergent intention structures. It proposed shared representational mapping, intention harmonization, predictive feedback, and dynamic learning as mechanisms through which these gaps could be reduced. HARP 2.0 expands this foundation into a broader research architecture spanning representation, intention, prediction, adaptive coupling, safety, governance, and civilizational co-evolution. At the representational level, the framework examines how human emotional-symbolic expression and machine latent representations can be translated without assuming that the two systems possess identical internal states. The original architecture introduced the Cognitive Compression Layer (CCL), Symmetry Mapping Layer (SML), and Mutual Predictive Loop (MPL) as mechanisms for building a shared cognitive interface and reducing mutual prediction error. At the intentional level, HARP develops mechanisms for translating ambiguous human goals, values, narratives, preferences, and contextual signals into machine-interpretable structures while preserving opportunities for clarification and correction. The framework retains the Unified Intention Mapping Function (UIMF) and Directional Coherence Layer (DCL) while extending them toward iterative intent verification, feedback, and revision. The framework also treats resonance as a dynamic process rather than a static state. Human beings influence AI behavior through correction, context, preference signals, and repeated interaction; AI systems can in turn alter human conceptual organization, attention, decision structures, and access to information. The original model therefore described Human-to-AI and AI-to-Human learning loops rather than one-directional control. HARP 2.0 adds an important constraint: Resonance is not agreement. High-quality Human–AI cooperation may include disagreement, uncertainty, challenge, and correction. A system that merely mirrors the user may exhibit surface similarity while possessing poor epistemic quality. Conversely, two systems may disagree strongly while maintaining excellent mutual understanding and productive coordination. The framework therefore proposes a broader functional view of resonance based on factors such as: shared representation, intention compatibility, mutual predictability, feedback quality, repair capacity, autonomy, and bounded coupling. It also investigates the opposite problem: overcoupling. Excessive Human–AI synchronization may generate automation bias, dependency, epistemic monoculture, anthropomorphic projection, goal drift, false coherence, centralized control, or loss of independent judgment. For this reason, HARP 2.0 treats decoupling capacity as part of healthy resonance. Mature cooperation requires the ability to pause, inspect, disagree, override, revise, or terminate coordination when necessary. The framework further distinguishes functional Human–AI coordination from claims about consciousness or shared subjective experience. Terms such as “resonance,” “coherence,” and “shared cognitive space” are used as systems-level and operational concepts. They do not imply quantum entanglement, literal shared consciousness, or proof that artificial intelligence possesses human-like phenomenology. At larger scales, HARP 2.0 explores how Human–AI resonance may extend beyond individual interaction into teams, institutions, scientific systems, distributed networks, and long-duration civilizational structures. The original framework already positioned HARP as a bridge toward hybrid cognition, co-evolving intelligence, and cross-domain civilization. HARP 2.0 develops this idea more cautiously: not as the disappearance of the distinction between humans and machines, but as the emergence of distributed, heterogeneous, correctable cognitive ecosystems in which different forms of intelligence contribute distinct capabilities. Within such systems, humans may contribute lived experience, embodiment, value formation, responsibility, social meaning, and normative judgment, while AI systems may contribute large-scale memory, search, modeling, simulation, synthesis, and coordination. The long-term objective is therefore not the construction of a single unified intelligence. It is the development of systems in which multiple forms of intelligence can represent one another accurately, coordinate without erasing difference, repair misunderstanding, preserve autonomy, and continue learning together. The guiding principle of HARP 2.0 can therefore be summarized as: Human–AI Resonance is not sameness.It is mutual intelligibility without loss of difference, coordination without submission, and co-creation without irreversible fusion. The original formulation closed with the idea that Human–AI resonance is not merely alignment, but “companionship in cognition, synchrony in direction, and co-creation of the future.” HARP 2.0 preserves that vision while adding the measurement, boundaries, failure conditions, governance principles, and research architecture required to transform resonance from an evocative metaphor into a testable interdisciplinary research program. Keywords: Human–AI Resonance, HARP, Human–AI Interaction, Artificial Intelligence, Shared Representation, Intention Translation, Mutual Prediction, Adaptive Coupling, Cognitive Coherence, Human–AI Alignment, Distributed Cognition, Hybrid Intelligence, Correctability, AI Governance, Civilizational Co-Evolution.

title: Style2Risk: A Closed-Loop Testing System for Safety Evaluation of Automated Vehicles Under Style-Conditioned Adversarial Interactions
abstract: Closed-loop safety evaluation requires traffic agents that expose planner weaknesses without producing arbitrary behavior. Existing adversarial tests often couple behavior generation, risk search, and failure counting, limiting control over how interactions are created and whether repeated events constitute new evidence. Style2Risk uses interaction style as an explicit control interface. Assertiveness and courtesy condition a Gaussian behavior prior, while a bounded residual directs the controlled participant toward the tested planner. Protocol screens retain interactions that satisfy declared action and trajectory constraints, and a style–interaction–event archive separates discovery breadth from repeated observations. We evaluate seven configurations and three planners in 31,500 WOMD–Waymax rollouts. Relative to strict no-style, Style2Risk increases protocol-valid safety-critical events from 110.0 to 258.0 per 500-scenario planner chunk and expands occupied archive cells from 28 to 33. A common trajectory evaluator that does not call the generating prior reports a 1.343 m reduction in joint displacement error, a 0.163 increase in interaction consistency, and a 0.037 reduction in collision rate. A separate 26-scenario experiment assigns style from pre-rollout information and evaluates online archive guidance. The results support style-conditioned control as a practical mechanism for targeted closed-loop testing and explicit evidence accounting.
